what_it_does: Modern server software has such a large set of instructions that the CPU frequently has to wait for instruction fetches — stalling the whole pipeline even when the data those instructions need is sitting ready in the cache. Garibaldi fixes this by teaching the last-level cache (the large shared cache chip that all CPU cores use) to recognize which instructions are paired with heavily-used data, protect those instructions from being evicted, and proactively fetch cold paired data when low-priority instructions miss. Added on top of an existing state-of-the-art cache policy, it improves server CPU performance by 13.2% on average.
method_in_detail:
The idea. A CPU has a hierarchy of caches to avoid slow trips to main memory. The last-level cache (LLC) is the largest and shared among all cores. Modern LLC policies are excellent at keeping frequently-used data in cache (they approximate the theoretically optimal eviction strategy). But they completely ignore instructions — and in server workloads, each instruction cache miss stalls the CPU's front end, delaying every subsequent data access that instruction would have triggered, even if all that data is already present in the cache. The paper calls this the 'instruction victim problem': hot data evicts cold instructions, and those cold instructions then gate access to the very hot data.

How it works. Garibaldi adds a 194KB pair table next to the LLC. Each entry maps an instruction cache line's physical address to a 6-bit 'miss cost' counter and the addresses of the data lines that instruction accesses. The counter is incremented when a data access triggered by that instruction hits in the cache (the instruction is valuable), and decremented when the data misses. At eviction time, if the LLC's normal policy wants to evict an instruction line, Garibaldi first queries the pair table; if the aged miss cost exceeds a dynamically adjusted threshold, the instruction is protected and the next candidate is evicted instead. For instructions that are not protected and subsequently miss, Garibaldi proactively fetches their paired cold data lines in parallel with the instruction fetch, overlapping two misses into one delay.

The key design choice. The protection threshold is adjusted every 100,000 LLC accesses by monitoring P(data miss | instruction miss) — the conditional probability that a data access fails when its triggering instruction was missing. If data is mostly hitting despite instruction misses, protection is too aggressive and the threshold rises; if data is also missing, more instructions should be protected and the threshold falls.

The result. Across 16 server workloads on a 40-core machine, Garibaldi on top of Mockingjay (the best existing LLC policy) achieves 13.2% geometric-mean speedup over LRU, versus 6.1% for Mockingjay alone, and reduces energy by 10.4%. Individual workloads improve up to 65%.
